title: Do ants hold conversations?
source_text: Ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ τοῖς ἀποθνῄσκουσιν μύρμηξί φησι τοὺς ζῶντας ἴδιόν τι ἀποκρίνειν χωρίον. κἀκεῖνο αὐτοῖς εἶναι πάτρια μνήματα, λεκτέον ὅτι ὅσῳ πλείονα λέγει τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων ἐγκώμια, τοσούτῳ πλεῖον. κἂν μὴ θέλῃ, αὔξει τὸ τοῦ πάντα κοσμήσαντος λόγου ἔργον καὶ δείκνυσι τὴν ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἐντρέχειαν, δυναμένην κοσμεῖν τῷ λόγῳ καὶ τὰ πλεονεκτήματα τῆς φύσεως τῶν ἀλόγων. (τί δὲ λέγω τῶν ἀλόγων.) ἐπεὶ Κέλσῳ δοκεῖ μηδ᾿ ἄλογα εἶναι τὰ κατὰ τὰς κοινὰς πάντων ἐννοίας ἄλογα καλούμενα; οὐδὲ τοὺς μύρμηκας γοῦν οἴεται εἶναι ἀλόγους ὁ περὶ τῆς ὅλης φύσεως ἐπαγγειλάμενος λέγειν καὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἐν τῇ ἐπιγραφῇ τοῦ βιβλίου αὐχήσας. φησὶ γὰρ περὶ τῶν μυρμήκων ὡς διαλεγομένων ἀλλήλοις τοιαῦτα· καὶ μὲν δὴ καὶ ἀπαντῶντες ἀλλήλοις διαλέγονται, ὅθεν οὐδὲ τῶν ὁδῶν ἁμαρτάνουσιν· οὐκοῦν καὶ λόγου συμπλήρωσίς ἐστι παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς καὶ κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι καθολικῶν τινων καὶ φωνὴ καὶ τυγχάνοντα καὶ σημαινόμενα. τὸ γὰρ διαλέγεσθαί τινα πρὸς ἕτερον ἐν φωνῇ γίνεται δηλούσῃ τι σημαινόμενον. πολλάκις δὲ καὶ περὶ τῶν καλουμένων τυγχανόντων ἀπαγγελλούσῃ· ἅπερ καὶ ἐν μύρμηξι λέγειν εἶναι πῶς οὐ πάντων ἂν εἴη καταγελαστότατον;
pass_a_gloss: Since he says also that for the ants dying (ἀποθνῄσκω) the living (ζῶντες) set apart (ἀποκρίνω) some proper/own (ἴδιος) place (χωρίον), and that for them is ancestral tombs (πάτρια μνήματα), it must be said (λεκτέον) that by as much as he speaks more eulogies (ἐγκώμιον) of the irrational animals, by so much more, even if he does not wish (θέλω), he increases (αὔξω) the work of the reason/Word (λόγος) that ordered (κοσμέω) all things, and shows (δείκνυμι) the skill/adroitness (ἐντρέχεια) in men, able to adorn/order (κοσμέω) by reason/speech (λόγος) even the advantages (πλεονέκτημα) of the nature of the irrational. (But why do I say 'of the irrational'?) Since it seems to Celsus that not even irrational are those called irrational according to the common notions (κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι) of all? Not even the ants at least does he think to be irrational, the one who professed (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) to speak about the whole nature and boasted (αὐχέω) of the truth (ἀλήθεια) in the title (ἐπιγραφή) of the book. For he says about the ants, as conversing (διαλέγομαι) with one another, such things: 'and indeed also meeting (ἀπαντάω) one another they converse, whence neither do they miss (ἁμαρτάνω) the roads (ὁδός); therefore there is also a completion/full complement (συμπλήρωσις) of reason among them, and common notions of certain universals (καθολικά), and utterance (φωνή) and objects (τυγχάνοντα) and things signified (σημαινόμενα).' For conversing of someone toward another comes about in an utterance making clear (δηλόω) some thing signified, and often also reporting (ἀπαγγέλλω) about the so-called objects; which things to say are also in ants, how would it not be most laughable (καταγελαστότατον) of all?
pass_b_english: Since he also says that the living “set apart a special place for the ants that die, and this serves them as ancestral tombs,” we must reply that the more he speaks in praise of irrational animals, the more, even against his will, he magnifies the work of the Word who set all things in order, and shows the skill that is in men, which can adorn in words even the advantages that irrational creatures have by nature.

But why do I say “irrational”? For Celsus thinks that the creatures which, by the common notions of all men, are called irrational are not irrational at all. At any rate he does not think even ants are irrational, this man who promised to speak about the whole of nature and boasted of truth in the title of his book. For he speaks of ants as conversing with one another, in these words: “And indeed, when they meet one another they converse, and that is why they do not lose their way. So there is among them a full measure of reason, common notions of certain universals, utterance, objects and meanings.”

For one person’s conversing with another takes place in an utterance that makes known some meaning, and often reports about what are called objects. To say that these exist among ants as well, how could that not be the most ridiculous thing of all?

choices.choice: Ants' tombs: indirect speech smoothed; idion choria -> 'a special place'; quotation marks kept around Celsus's reported words
Reordered 'creatures which, by the common notions of all men, are called irrational' so the phrase attaches to 'called'; 'not even irrational' -> 'not irrational at all'

Both Celsus passages (ants' tombs; ants conversing) are given in quotation marks; the first is indirect speech in the Greek. τοῦ πάντα κοσμήσαντος λόγου: λόγος can be 'reason' or the divine 'Word'; given 4.81 (the most ancient Word made irrational nature), I take it as the Word and capitalise it. κοσμεῖν τῷ λόγῳ is taken as 'adorn in words', since Celsus's own eloquent eulogy displays human skill; 'set in order by reason' is also possible. The title Celsus boasted of is his 'True Doctrine' (Ἀληθὴς Λόγος). φωνή, τυγχάνοντα and σημαινόμενα are Stoic terms of meaning (the spoken sound, the actual external object, the thing signified); rendered 'utterance, objects and meanings'. 'The common notions of all' (κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι) is also Stoic language. The parenthesis 'But why do I say irrational?' is Koetschau's punctuation. No Scripture quoted or alluded to.
